bg_facts: Binance says the break in began with fake job interviews.
An internal AI tool helped the attackers reach more engineers.

slides.title: What *happened*
slides.body: On November 3, Binance shared its first report on the October 29 theft of about $6.3 billion in crypto. It says the break in started with a fake job interview.

slides.title: How they *got in*
slides.body: Binance says attackers used fake recruitment interviews and malicious downloads to take over an engineer's company computer. It calls this a long, multi step attack, not one simple phishing email.

slides.title: The *AI tool* part
slides.body: On October 20, using that computer as a springboard, the attackers used Binance's own internal AI tool to take over two more engineers. With their logins they reached the system that signs wallet transfers.

slides.title: Who and *the money*
slides.body: The FBI says North Korean hackers it calls TraderTraitor did it. About $3 billion has been frozen. Binance says it will cover all losses for customers.

slides.title: What Binance *did*
slides.body: It replaced the affected devices, cancelled the engineers' logins and tokens, rebuilt the wallet system in a new environment and tightened access to its internal AI tools. The investigation is still going.

slides.title: What it means *for you*
slides.body: Run a business? Never open a test file or download from a recruiter or stranger on a work computer. Give staff and AI tools only the access they need. Use app based two factor login everywhere.
